summary: States the IETF consensus that standard protocols must use appropriate strong security mechanisms, and gives the history and rationale behind that rule. It establishes this requirement as a best current practice.

eli5.summary: The people who write internet rules decided every new rule must come with good locks. This document explains why and says so officially.

what is the strong security requirement
difference between must implement and must use
is encryption required in ietf protocols
subtitle: The IETF's rule that standard protocols must implement appropriate strong security, and the history behind it.

tldr.problem: Protocols designed for protected networks often end up on the global Internet, where nobody provides security for them and users find themselves vulnerable to attack.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC records the IETF consensus, known as the Danvers Doctrine, that IETF standard protocols MUST implement appropriate strong security mechanisms, while leaving users free to turn those mechanisms off.
tldr.outcome: It makes strong security a mandatory-to-implement requirement for IETF standard protocols and gives it the status of a best current practice. It is not obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

facts.label: Core rule
facts.value: Security is MUST implement, not MUST use

today: RFC 3365 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 61) and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It remains the IETF's written statement of the strong security requirement for standard protocols.

sections.title: Why the IETF Cares About Security
sections.content:
The Internet is a global network of independently managed networks and hosts. No central authority runs it, and none is responsible for providing security across it either. Security therefore has to be provided end-to-end or host to host.

The IETF's security role, as this RFC puts it, is to make sure that IETF standard protocols have the features needed to provide appropriate security for the application as it may be used across the Internet. Mandatory-to-implement mechanisms should give enough security to protect sensitive business applications.

The RFC uses MUST, SHOULD and MAY as defined in RFC 2119, even though it does not define a protocol.
sections.eli5: Nobody is in charge of the whole internet, so nobody puts locks on it for you. The people who design the rules have to build the locks into the rules themselves.

sections.title: Three Security Services
sections.content:
The RFC borrows definitions from the Internet Security Glossary (RFC 2828) for three essential services.

  • Authentication verifies an identity claimed by or for a process, computer system or person. At the internetwork layer that includes checking that a datagram came from where it claims to.
  • Data confidentiality protects data against disclosure to unauthorized individuals or processes. The text says Internet Standards Documents SHOULD NOT use it as a synonym for privacy, which is a different concept.
  • Data integrity protects against unauthorized changes to data, intentional or accidental, by making sure that changes are detectable.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of protection: knowing who you are really talking to, keeping your message secret, and making sure nobody changed it on the way.

sections.title: Why Protected Environments Do Not Last
sections.content:
The Internet provides no inherent security. Some enclaves exist where users believe the environment itself provides it, such as a company network not connected to the global Internet. One might think protocols built for such an enclave need no security services.

The RFC says history has shown otherwise: applications that use the TCP/IP protocol suite wind up being used over the Internet, even when they were never meant for a wide area environment. If an application does not provide security, its users discover that they are vulnerable to attack.

Section 5 adds that the IETF already has security tools. IPsec (RFC 2411) and TLS (RFC 2246) are two well known protocols, while SASL (RFC 2222) and GSSAPI (RFC 2743) work as toolkits inside another protocol. Designers must choose whether to reuse a protocol, build their own on a standard tool, or do something else entirely. The Security Considerations section is where they document the threats and the logic of the design.
sections.eli5: People often build something for a safe little clubhouse, then it ends up out on the busy street. If it has no locks, everyone finds out the hard way.

sections.title: The Danvers Doctrine
sections.content:
At the 32cd IETF in Danvers, Massachusetts, in April 1995, the IESG asked the plenary for a consensus on how strong the security in IETF standards should be. The immediate question was whether to support "export" grade security, which means weak security, but it raised the general issue of security.

The overwhelming consensus was that the IETF should standardize on the best security available, regardless of national policies. This is often called the Danvers Doctrine. Over time its interpretation was extended to mean that all IETF protocols should operate securely.

The RFC notes that since 1995 the Internet has come under increasing attack, and it mentions the Distributed Denial of Service attacks that drew press coverage in 2000. Its conclusion is that failing to provide secure protocols makes the Internet less useful as an international communications infrastructure. Because it is hard to predict how a protocol will be used, the RFC concludes that the IETF MUST implement strong security in all protocols.
sections.eli5: A long time ago, a big group of rule writers voted to always use the best locks available. Later they decided that applies to every rule they write.

sections.title: MUST Implement Versus MUST Use
sections.content:
The RFC separates two ideas. Security is a MUST implement, but that is different from MUST use. Some protocols run in secure enclaves where security processing may add a significant performance cost, so it is reasonable for the end user to be able to disable security features. Here "end user" includes any deployer of a technology, even a whole enterprise.

Security must still be a MUST implement, so that users have the option of enabling it when the situation calls for it.

Implementors must build the security in. Deployers decide whether to switch it on.
sections.eli5: Every bike must be sold with a lock. Whether you actually lock it in your own garage is up to you, but the lock has to be there.

sections.title: Encryption, Confidentiality and Common Objections
sections.content:
Is encryption a MUST? The RFC says not necessarily. Many people equate encryption with confidentiality, but which services fit depends on the application. Its example is building control: instructions to open and close heat vents probably need no confidentiality, but authentication and integrity matter so that a malicious actor cannot raise or lower the temperature at will.

So "MUST we implement confidentiality?" gets the answer "depends", while "MUST we make use of cryptographic technology?" gets "likely", since authentication and integrity usually need it.

Section 9 answers three objections to cryptography. Export control is becoming less of a concern in most of the developed world, and where it remains it is about confidentiality, not cryptography itself. Performance is an engineering problem to minimize. And designers need not become cryptographers, because they can use existing well understood ciphers and cipher suites. The Security Area aims to produce guides for choosing technology.
sections.eli5: Not every message needs to be secret. A note telling a heater to turn on does not need hiding, but you do want to be sure nobody fake sent it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is a single remark: the document is about the IETF's requirement that security be considered in the implementation of protocols, so it is entirely about security. It adds no further security analysis.
sections.eli5: This whole document is about security, so there is nothing extra to add at the end.
